questions.question: Which of the following structural abnormalities is most commonly associated with the given image?

options.A: Malformation of the vertebral arches
options.B: Incomplete development of the basichondrocranium
options.C: Herniation of brain tissue through the skull
options.D: Fusion of the cranial sutures

explanation.text: Anencephaly is associated with severe abnormalities in the base of the skull (basichondrocranium), affecting its shape, position, and ossification. Anencephaly: Neurulation failure: Anencephaly occurs when the neural tube fuses in the spinal cord (Caudal neuropore) but fails to fuse in the brain region (Cranial neuropore), leading to missing parts of the brain and skull.

The cranial and caudal neuropores close around day 25 and 28 of development respectively in a normally developing fetus. Types of Neural Tube Defects: Neural Tube Defect Description Anencephaly (Cranioschisis) Failure of neural tube fusion in the brain region, results in missing parts of the brain and skull. Craniorachischisis Totalis Complete failure of the neural tube to fuse, affecting both the brain and spinal cord.
Spina Bifida Incomplete fusion of the spinal neural tube or failure of formation of vertebral arches leads to defects in the spinal cord. Malformation of the vertebral arches (Option A):
This is characteristic of spina bifida, not anencephaly.
**Herniation of brain tissue through the skull (Option C):** This describes encephalocele, a different neural tube defect, not anencephaly.
**Fusion of the cranial sutures (Option D):** This refers to craniosynostosis, which is not related to anencephaly.

questions.question: Which of the following is a common feature of craniorachischisis compared to rachischisis?

options.A: Craniorachischisis results from failure of caudal neural tube closure, while rachischisis affects the entire tube.
options.B: Craniorachischisis exposes both the brain and spinal cord; rachischisis exposes only the spinal cord.
options.C: Craniorachischisis is less severe than rachischisis and affects only the vertebrae.
options.D: Craniorachischisis involves complete neural tube closure, while rachischisis exposes both the brain and spinal cord.

explanation.text: This option correctly identifies the extent of exposure associated with each condition, with craniorachischisis being more severe and involving both structures. Rachischisis and Craniorachischisis: Condition Rachischisis Craniorachischisis Description A type of spina bifida where a portion of the spinal cord remains open. The most severe form of neural tube defect- involving exposure of both the brain and spinal cord.

Neural Tube Involvement Occurs due to the failure of fusion of the caudal portion of the neural tube. (Option A) Occurs due to the failure of fusion of both the cranial as well as the caudal portions of the neural tube. (Option D) Severity Severe, but localised to the spinal cord Most severe (Option C) Exposure Spinal cord neural tissue is exposed Both the brain and spinal cord are exposed. Diagram

questions.question: Which of the following statements about spina bifida is false?

options.A: Spina bifida occulta presents with an abnormal U or V shape in the vertebrae.
options.B: Meningocele involves protrusion of the meninges and spinal cord through the defect.
options.C: Diastematomyelia is rarely associated with spina bifida and splits the spinal cord.
options.D: The incidence of myelomeningocele has decreased due to prenatal diagnosis and termination options.

explanation.text: Meningocele involves only the protrusion of the meninges, not the spinal cord. When the spinal cord is also involved, the condition is called myelomeningocele. Spina bifida is a birth defect where the neural tube fails to close properly, affecting the caudal portion of the spinal neural tube.

Types: Type Description Spina Bifida Cystica Involves a visible sac or cyst containing the spinal cord or nerves protruding from the back.Two types: Meningocele: A sac containing only the meninges and CSF, with the spinal cord intact. Myelomeningocele: Sac contains both the meninges and a portion of the spinal cord; the most severe form.

Spina Bifida Occulta The defect is hidden under the skin, typically found in the lumbosacral or sacral regions; it affects ~5% of the population. Impact on Spinal Cord Development: Impact Description Ascent of the Conus Medullaris The conus medullaris normally ascends relative to the vertebral column. In spina bifida, this ascent is impaired, leading to a tethered cord.

Tethered Cord The spinal cord is anchored at the defect site, restricting normal upward movement, which can cause neurological complications. Diastematomyelia An extremely rare condition where the spinal cord is split into two columns by a bony or cartilaginous spur, often associated with tethered cord. (Option C) Prenatal Diagnosis: Detection: Spina bifida can be identified through ultrasound imaging during pregnancy.

Spina Bifida Occulta Indicator: The posterior ossification centres of the vertebrae may display an abnormal U or V shape. (Option A) Incidence: The prevalence of severe types, such as myelomeningocele, has decreased due to improved prenatal diagnosis and options for termination. (Option D)

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a brain region with its corresponding structure or function?

options.A: Myelencephalon: Develops into the cerebellum, involved in motor control and balance.
options.B: Tectum: Located in the hindbrain and responsible for auditory and visual reflexes.
options.C: Hypothalamus: Part of the diencephalon, regulates hunger, thirst, body temperature, and sleep-wake cycles.
options.D: Frontal Lobe: Primarily involved in visual processing and spatial awareness.

explanation.text: Parts of the Brain: Brain Region Components Functions/Derivatives Prosencephalon (Forebrain) Diencephalon Relay centre for sensory information, regulates endocrine system, autonomic functions Thalamus Relays sensory information to the cerebral cortex.

Hypothalamus Regulates hunger, thirst, temperature, sleep-wake cycles, endocrine system Epithalamus The pineal gland (melatonin production) Subthalamus Involved in motor control Telencephalon Forms cerebral hemispheres, median part in front of the interventricular foramen and lateral ventricle Cerebral Cortex Higher cognitive functions (language, memory, reasoning, movement) Frontal Lobe (Option D) Planning, decision-making, problem-solving, voluntary movement Parietal Lobe Sensory information, spatial awareness, navigation Temporal Lobe Auditory processing, language comprehension Occipital Lobe Visual processing Lateral Ventricles Fluid-filled cavities for cerebrospinal fluid circulation Mesencephalon (Midbrain) Cerebral Peduncles Connects cerebrum to the brainstem Tectum (Option B) Made of superior and inferior colliculi.
Tegmentum Contains nuclei of 5,6,7,8 nerves.

**Rhombencephalon (Hindbrain) Myelencephalon (Option A):** Develops into the medulla oblongata (breathing, heart rate) Metencephalon Forms the pons (signal relay) and cerebellum (motor control, balance)

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the treatment of aqueduct stenosis is correct?

options.A: Ventriculoperitoneal shunting permanently cures aqueduct stenosis.
options.B: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy involves diverting CSF to the abdominal cavity.
options.C: Aqueduct stenosis can be treated with medications alone in most cases.
options.D: Ventriculoperitoneal shunting involves diverting CSF to reduce intracranial pressure.

explanation.text: Ventriculoperitoneal shunting diverts CSF to relieve pressure caused by hydrocephalus. Aqueduct Stenosis: Category Details Causes Congenital: Developmental anomalies Acquired: Tumours, infections, trauma Symptoms Headache, nausea, vomiting (Due to CSF accumulation) Cognitive impairments due to increased intracranial pressure. Diagnosis MRI or CT scans showing aqueduct narrowing and ventricular enlargement.

Treatment Ventriculoperitoneal shunting: Diverts excess CSF (Option A) Endoscopic third ventriculostomy: Bypasses obstruction (high relapse rate) (Option B) Aqueduct stenosis can be treated with medications alone in most cases (Option C): It usually requires surgical intervention, as medications alone are not sufficient.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the cerebellar peduncles and corpora quadrigemina is correct?

options.A: Superior cerebellar peduncles carry afferent signals from the cerebellum to the medulla.
options.B: Middle cerebellar peduncles transmit sensory information from the spinal cord to the cerebellum.
options.C: Inferior cerebellar peduncles connect the cerebellum to the medulla and aid in balance and posture.
options.D: Superior colliculi are involved in auditory processing and relay signals to the auditory cortex.

explanation.text: The inferior cerebellar peduncles carry both afferent and efferent fibres, connecting the cerebellum to the medulla oblongata and playing a role in balance and posture control. Cerebellar Peduncles Peduncle Function Components Role Superior Cerebellar Peduncles Carry efferent (outgoing) signals from the cerebellum to the midbrain. (Option A) Connects the cerebellum to the midbrain.

It contains axons from the Dentate, Emboliform and the Globose nuclei of the cerebellum. Movement planning and coordination. Middle Cerebellar Peduncles The main route for afferent (incoming) signals to the cerebellum. Connects cerebellum to the pons. (Option B)
Provides information about planned movements.

**Inferior Cerebellar Peduncles (Option C):** Carry both afferent and efferent fibres. Connects cerebellum to the medulla oblongata. It contains axons from the fastigial nucleus of the cerebellum. Receives sensory information for balance and posture, and sends signals to vestibular nuclei and reticular formation. Corpora Quadrigemina (Tectum) Colliculi Function Components Role Superior Colliculi Involved in visual processing and eye movement control. (Option D) Receives input from optic nerves and visual processing areas. Coordinates head and eye movements in response to visual stimuli. Inferior Colliculi Plays a role in auditory processing. [musIC- Inferior Colliculus] Receives input from auditory pathways. Projects to the medial geniculate nucleus of the thalamus for auditory signal relay.

questions.question: Identify the labelled structures in the given diagram.

options.A: A- Fornix; B- Hippocampus; C- Corpus Callosum
options.B: A – Fornix; B – Amygdala; C – Hippocampus
options.C: A- Fornix; B- Corpus Callosum; C- Hippocampus
options.D: A – Fornix; B – Hypothalamus; C – Amygdala

explanation.text: The diagram above shows the thalamus and the structures surrounding it. Structure Description Thalamus Grey matter mass; sensory and motor roles Fornix A c-shaped fibre bundle; connects the hippocampal formations of the two sides. The main efferent tract of the hippocampus. Corpus Callosum The largest commissure of the brain; links the cerebra hemispheres.

Caudate Nucleus The comma-shaped nucleus of the basal ganglia Choroid Plexus Produces CSF; vascular network. Hippocampus Seahorse-shaped (Curved and elongated); stores long-term memory and is a part of the limbic system.

questions.question: Which of the following accurately describes the pathway of the Papez circuit?

options.A: Cingulate cortex → Hippocampus → Mammillary bodies → Anterior thalamic nuclei → Fornix
options.B: Cingulate cortex → Mammillary bodies → Hippocampus → Fornix → Anterior thalamic nuclei
options.C: Hippocampus → Cingulate cortex → Anterior thalamic nuclei → Mammillary bodies → Fornix
options.D: Hippocampus → Fornix → Mammillary bodies → Anterior thalamic nuclei → Cingulate cortex

explanation.text: The Papez circuit starts in the hippocampus, travels through the fornix to the mammillary bodies, then to the anterior thalamic nuclei, and finally projects back to the cingulate cortex. Papez circuit: It is a part of the Limbic system. Fornix is a collection of axons. Fornix takes the information from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus, to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus (mammilo–thalamic tract).

From the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, the pathway comes back to the hippocampus, thus completing the circuit. Lesions in the Papez circuit occur in Alzheimer's disease and in alcoholics with vitamin B1 deficiency, leading to Korsakoff's psychosis characterized by anterograde amnesia, confabulation, confusion and disorientation

questions.question: A 5 year old child presents with developmental delays, including difficulties in motor coordination and speech. MRI reveals a complete absence of the corpus callosum. Which of the following is not typically associated with this condition?

options.A: Intellectual disability
options.B: Seizures
options.C: Hemispatial neglect
options.D: Hyperactivity and impulsivity

explanation.text: Hemispatial neglect is not typically associated with agenesis of the corpus callosum. Hemispatial neglect is often seen in patients with damage to one hemisphere, particularly the right hemisphere, leading to inattention to the opposite side of space (usually the left). In agenesis, both hemispheres may function independently, so hemispatial neglect is not a hallmark of this condition.

Agenesis of the corpus callosum is a rare congenital condition in which the corpus callosum, the structure connecting the two cerebral hemispheres, fails to develop properly or is absent. This can lead to a range of neurological and developmental issues. Causes: Genetic: Chromosomal abnormalities (e.g., trisomy 13, 18) or mutations in specific genes. Environmental: Prenatal factors like infections, alcohol, or drug exposure.

Clinical Features: Developmental delays: Intellectual disability, motor delays, and speech impairments. Seizures: Common due to lack of communication between brain hemispheres. Motor problems: Coordination issues, ataxia. Behavioral issues: Hyperactivity, impulsivity, and autistic-like behaviors. Cognitive challenges: Attention deficits and difficulty with higher cognitive functions.
Associated Conditions: Aicardi syndrome, Andermann syndrome, holoprosencephaly, fetal alcohol syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is part of the complete syndrome triad associated with Anterior Choroidal Artery Syndrome?

options.A: Bilateral hemiplegia
options.B: Contralateral hemisensory loss
options.C: Bitemporal hemianopia
options.D: Ipsilateral homonymous hemianopia

explanation.text: Anterior choroidal artery syndrome is associated with the clinical triad of contralateral hemiplegia, contralateral hemisensory loss and contralateral homonymous hemianopia Anterior Choroidal Artery Syndrome: Cause: Infarction in the anterior choroidal artery territory. Pathophysiology: AChA anastomoses with posterior choroidal artery and posterior cerebral artery.

Infarction occurs in the posterior limb of the internal capsule due to a lack of collateral supply. Complete syndrome triad: Contralateral hemiplegia - Weakness or paralysis on one side of the body opposite to brain injury. (Option A) Contralateral hemisensory loss - Loss of sensation on one side of the body opposite to brain injury.

Contralateral homonymous hemianopia - Loss of the same visual field (either right or left) in both eyes, opposite to the side of brain damage. (Options C and D) Homonymous quadruple sectoranopia if the lateral geniculate body is involved. Incongruent homonymous hemianopia if the optic tract is involved. Neuropsychological associations: Left neglect syndrome in right-sided lesions. Language disorders in left-sided lesions.

questions.question: The labyrinthine artery arises from which of the following arteries?

options.A: Internal carotid artery
options.B: External carotid artery
options.C: Vertebral artery
options.D: Basilar artery

explanation.text: Labyrinthine artery is a long, slender branch that typically originates from either the basilar artery or the anterior-inferior cerebellar artery. It travels alongside the vestibulocochlear nerve and passes through the internal auditory meatus to supply blood to the inner ear. It is an end artery.

questions.question: In the image below, which structure is labeled as the rostrum of the corpus callosum?

options.A: Structure A
options.B: Structure B
options.C: Structure C
options.D: Structure D

explanation.text: The corpus callosum is the largest commissure of the brain. It is divided from before backwards into the following four parts: Genu: This is the thick, curved front part of the corpus callosum, located about 4 cm behind the front of the brain. Its fibers curve forward into the front parts of the frontal lobes, forming a fork-like shape known as the forceps minor.

Rostrum: The genu extends downward and backward as a thin extension called the rostrum, which connects to the lamina terminalis. Body: It is the central part of the corpus callosum, situated between the front (genu) and back (splenium) parts. Splenium: The splenium is the large, back part of the corpus callosum, located about 6 cm in front of the occipital region.

Its fibers connect the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes of both brain hemispheres. The fibers connecting the occipital lobes form another fork-like shape known as the forceps major. Function: The corpus callosum is largely responsible for interhemispheric transfer of information which is essential for bilateral responses and learning processes.

questions.question: A 35 year old patient presents with rapid weight gain and persistent hunger despite adequate food intake. MRI reveals a lesion in the hypothalamus. Which of the following hypothalamic nuclei, when lesioned, is most likely to cause an uncontrolled appetite and extreme obesity?

options.A: Anterior Hypothalamic Area
options.B: Ventromedial nucleus
options.C: Lateral hypothalamus
options.D: Suprachiasmatic Nucleus

explanation.text: Lesions in the ventromedial nucleus of the hypothalamus are known to lead to uncontrolled appetite and extreme obesity, as this area is critical for satiety and regulating food intake.

Hypothalamic Nuclei and Effects of Lesions Area/Nuclei Function Lesion Anterior Hypothalamic Area & Preoptic Area (Option A) Influences parasympathetic responses (e.g., lowers blood pressure, slows heart rate, heat regulation) Can disrupt thermoregulation and lead to hyperthermia. Posterior & Lateral Nuclei Mediates sympathetic responses (e.g., increases blood pressure, accelerates heart rate, cold regulation).
May cause impaired sympathetic responses and issues with stress response.

**Lateral Hypothalamus (Option C):** Acts as the hunger & thirst centre; stimulates food intake. Leads to anorexia and significant weight loss. Medial Hypothalamus- Ventromedial nucleus Acts as the satiety centre; inhibits eating. Causes uncontrolled appetite and extreme obesity. Supraoptic & Paraventricular Nuclei Secretes vasopressin and oxytocin; regulates water balance and reproductive functions. Can disrupt water balance and lead to diabetes insipidus.
**Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (Option D):** Regulates circadian rhythms and biological clocks. Can disrupt sleep-wake cycles and lead to insomnia.

questions.question: Which of the following is the function of the Ventral Posteromedial Nucleus within the Ventral Group Nuclei?

options.A: Influences motor activities by connecting with the premotor cortex.
options.B: Receives sensory information from the cerebellum and red nucleus.
options.C: Receives trigeminal and gustatory pathways.
options.D: Projects to the primary motor areas of the cerebral cortex.

explanation.text: The Ventral Posteromedial Nucleus receives trigeminal and gustatory pathways which are responsible for processing sensory information from the face. Ventral Group Nuclei Ventral Anterior Nucleus: Connects to the reticular formation, substantia nigra, corpus striatum, and premotor cortex Influences motor cortex activities. (Option A) Ventral Lateral Nucleus: Similar connections to the ventral anterior nucleus.

**Receives input from the cerebellum and red nucleus (Option B):** Projects to motor and premotor areas. (Option D) Ventral Posterior Nucleus: Subdivided into: Ventral Posteromedial Nucleus: Receives trigeminal and gustatory pathways. Ventral Posterolateral Nucleus: Receives sensory tracts; projects to primary somatic sensory areas in the postcentral gyrus (BA 1, 2, 3)

questions.question: Which of the following thalamic nuclei is concerned with recent memory and emotional tone?

options.A: Medial geniculate body
options.B: Anterior Thalamic Nuclei
options.C: Dorsomedial Nucleus
options.D: Lateral geniculate body

explanation.text: Anterior Thalamic Nuclei are directly connected to the limbic system and play a crucial role in emotional tone and mechanisms of recent memory. Thalamic Nuclei: Anterior part Medial part Lateral part Contains anterior thalamic nuclei. Receives mammillothalamic tract from mammillary nuclei. Reciprocal connections with cingulate gyrus and hypothalamus. Functions related to the limbic system. Concerned with emotional tone and recent memory.

It is a part of the Papez circuit Contains the large dorsomedial nucleus and smaller nuclei. Two-way connections with prefrontal cortex and hypothalamic nuclei. Interconnected with all other thalamic nuclei. Responsible for integrating sensory (somatic, visceral, olfactory) information with emotional and subjective states. (Option C) Subdivided into dorsal and ventral tiers.
Dorsal Tier: Includes lateral dorsal nucleus, lateral posterior nucleus, and pulvinar. Interconnections with other thalamic nuclei, parietal lobe, cingulate gyrus, occipital, and temporal lobes.

Ventral Tier: Nuclei arranged in a craniocaudal sequence Further divided into ventral anterior, ventral posterior and ventral lateral nuclei Other Thalamic Nuclei Intralaminar Nuclei: Influence consciousness and alertness; receive input from the reticular formation. Midline Nuclei: Functions unclear; receive afferent fibres from the reticular formation. Reticular Nucleus: Regulates thalamic activity; connects to other thalamic nuclei.
Medial Geniculate Body: Processes auditory information; projects to the auditory cortex. (Option A) Lateral Geniculate Body: Processes visual input; projects to the visual cortex. (Option D)

questions.question: A 62 year old patient presents with sudden onset of right-sided weakness and facial droop. Neurological examination reveals upper motor neuron signs with weakness in both the arm and leg on the right side. MRI confirms an infarct in the middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory involving the genu of the internal capsule. Which of the following tracts passes through the genu?

options.A: Corticobulbar tract
options.B: Corticospinal tract
options.C: Spinothalamic tract
options.D: Medial lemniscus

explanation.text: The genu of the internal capsule contains the corticobulbar tract (corticonuclear tract), which is responsible for motor control of the cranial nerves, especially facial movements. Damage here can result in facial weakness, as seen in the patient.

Blood Supply of the Internal Capsule: Artery Supplies Tracts Affected in Lesions Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) The ventral part of the anterior limb Corticopontine tract affecting communication between cortex and cerebellum Heubner's Artery Ventral anterior limb Corticopontine and frontopontine tracts: Impaired voluntary movements.

Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) Parts of the anterior limb Genu Posterior limb Corticobulbar tract (genu): Facial muscle weakness and motor deficits in cranial nerves Corticospinal tract (posterior limb): Contralateral limb weakness or paralysis (Option B) Internal Carotid Artery (ICA) - Varies depending on perforator origin, affecting similar tracts as MCA and AChA supplies Anterior Choroidal Artery (AChA) Ventral posterior limb Retro-lenticular Sub-lenticular portions Corticospinal tract (posterior limb): Contralateral motor deficits Optic radiations (retro-lenticular part): Visual field defects Auditory radiations (sub lenticular part): Auditory processing issues Spinothalamic tract (Option C): This tract is responsible for transmitting pain and temperature sensations from the body to the brain.
It does not pass through the genu of the internal capsule.
**Medial lemniscus (Option D):** This tract carries proprioception and vibration sense from the body to the brain, passing through the brainstem, not the genu of the internal capsule.

questions.question: Which of the following tracts passes through the genu of the internal capsule?

options.A: Corticospinal tract
options.B: Corticonuclear tract
options.C: Optic radiation
options.D: Auditory radiation

explanation.text: The corticonuclear tract, which contains motor fibres to cranial nerve motor nuclei, specifically passes through the genu of the internal capsule. Tracts Passing Through Internal Capsule: Genu: Corticonuclear tract (motor fibres to cranial nerve motor nuclei). Posterior Limb: Corticospinal tract (motor fibres to the contralateral spinal cord) (Option A). Corticopontine fibres from the parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes.

Fibres for the upper limb (anteriorly) and trunk/lower limbs (posteriorly). Superior Thalamic Peduncle (through anterior and posterior limbs): From ventral posterior and lateral posterior thalamic nuclei to parietal cortex (sensory areas).

Other Tracts Passing Through the Internal Capsule: Anterior limb Retrolentiform part Sublentiform part Frontopontine fibres (Arnold's bundle) Corticorubral fibres Parietopontine,occipitopontine, and occipitotectal fibres Optic radiation (Option C) Temporopontine fibres Auditory radiation (fibres from the medial geniculate body to the auditory cortex) (Option D) Thalamic fibres to the temporal cortex and amygdala.

questions.question: Which sulcus is involved in separating the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe?

options.A: Lateral Sulcus
options.B: Central Sulcus
options.C: Calcarine Sulcus
options.D: Parieto-occipital Sulcus

explanation.text: The central sulcus separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe. It runs roughly from the top of the brain down towards the lateral sulcus.

Lobes of the Cerebrum Frontal Lobe Temporal Lobe Parietal Lobe Occipital Lobe Sulci of the Cerebrum Lateral Sulcus: Seen laterally; separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes. (Option A) Central Sulcus: Runs Antero-inferiorly; separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe; visible laterally and medially.

Calcarine Sulcus: Visible medially; located in the occipital lobe, associated with the visual cortex. (Option C) Parieto-occipital Sulcus: Seen medially; separates the parietal and occipital lobes. (Option D) Lateral View Medial View Central Sulcus: Divides the frontal lobe (anterior) from the parietal lobe (posterior). Lateral Sulcus: Distinguishes the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.

Pre-central Gyrus: Located in front of the central sulcus; it contains the frontal motor cortex, which controls skeletal muscles. Post-central Gyrus: Located behind the central sulcus; houses the parietal sensory cortex for general sensations (touch, pain, temperature, proprioception). Insula: Found in the floor of the lateral sulcus. Central Sulcus: Separates the frontal motor cortex (pre-central gyrus) from the parietal sensory cortex.

Paracentral Lobule: Controls the contralateral lower limb, pelvis, and perineum. Calcarine Sulcus: Associated with the occipital visual cortex. Limbic Lobe: Involved in emotions and memory. Cingulate Gyrus: An arch-shaped convolution above the corpus callosum. Cerebral Cortex Layers and Functions: Has six layers of neurons. Layer Function I- Molecular layer Receives nonspecific input signals from lower brain centers.

Control the excitability of stimulated areas. II- External granular layer Receives nonspecific input and sends axons to the opposite cortex through the corpus callosum. III- External pyramidal layer Sends axons to related cortical areas on the opposite side through the corpus callosum. The outer band of Baillarger is a part of this layer of cerebral cortex, specifically located in the motor cortex and somatosensory cortex.

IV- Internal granular layer The primary layer for receiving input sensory signals, which then spread to the surface and deeper layers. V- Internal pyramidal layer Sends large axons to distant nervous system parts like basal ganglia, brain stem, and spinal cord. Controls signal transmission. VI-
Fusiform/ polymorphic layer Sends axons to the thalamus. Regulates excitability of incoming sensory signals.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the anatomical relations of the internal capsule?

options.A: The anterior limb lies between the thalamus and the posterior part of the lentiform nucleus.
options.B: The genu is located posterior to the head of the caudate nucleus.
options.C: The medial boundary consists of the thalamus and the caudate nucleus.
options.D: The retro lentiform part is situated above the lentiform nucleus.

explanation.text: The internal capsule is positioned medially next to both the thalamus and the caudate nucleus Internal Capsule The internal capsule is a compact bundle of projection fibres that connects the cerebral cortex with subcortical centres such as the thalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord. It contains both afferent (sensory) fibres from the thalamus to the cortex and efferent (motor) fibres from the cortex to the cerebral peduncle and midbrain.

Relations of Internal Capsule Medially: Thalamus and caudate nucleus Laterally: Lentiform nucleus Anterior limb: Between the head of the caudate nucleus and the anterior part of the lentiform nucleus (Option A) Posterior limb: Between the thalamus and the posterior part of the lentiform nucleus.
Genu: Bend between the anterior and posterior limbs, concave laterally (Option B) Retrolentiform part: Behind the lentiform nucleus (Option D) Sublentiform part: Below the lentiform nucleus.

questions.question: Match the following:

options.A: A-Putamen; B- Globus Pallidus; C- Caudate Nucleus; D- Subthalamic Nucleus; E- Substantia Nigra; F- Thalamus
options.B: A- Caudate Nucleus; B- Putamen; C- Thalamus; D- Globus Pallidus; E- Subthalamic Nucleus; F- Substantia Nigra
options.C: A- Caudate Nucleus; B- Globus Pallidus; C- Substantia Nigra; D- Globus Pallidus; E- Thalamus; F- Subthalamic Nucleus
options.D: A- Caudate Nucleus; B- Putamen; C- Globus Pallidus; D- Thalamus; E- Subthalamic Nucleus; F- Substantia Nigra

explanation.text: The basal ganglia work together to control movement by balancing excitatory and inhibitory signals. They help to initiate, plan, and execute movements, as well as to suppress unwanted movements. Dysfunctions in the basal ganglia can lead to various movement disorders, such as Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and Tourette syndrome.
